analysis_markdown:
# 2018 — FIRST POWER UP

## Read the game as control of time and access

POWER UP is a one-piece-possession game about establishing and preserving ownership of a shared scale and an alliance-specific switch. A cube is an investment in future scoring time, not a fixed number of points. The best action depends on the current balance, expected remaining ownership, where the next available cube is, and what the opponent can do while you travel. This makes a raw cubes-per-match ranking an incomplete description of robot value.

The governing source for the rules in this chapter is the [official 133-page manual](https://firstfrc.blob.core.windows.net/frc2018/Manual/2018FRCGameSeasonManual.pdf), especially physical PDF pages 33, 37–42 and 51–59. Section revision labels differ within the assembled PDF; do not call it an unchanging kickoff ruleset. This chapter is a retrospective architecture study, not a substitute for checking team updates or Q&A for a particular event. Numeric examples below are calculations or hypothetical scenarios, not reconstructed match observations.

A match has 15 seconds of autonomous play and 135 seconds of teleop, with the last 30 seconds designated endgame. Autonomous ownership is worth an initial 2 points and 2 per additional second; teleop ownership is worth an initial 1 and 1 per additional second, subject to powerups. Each autonomous line crossing earns 5 points. Each cube placed in the vault earns 5 points. Parking is 5 and climbing is 30 per qualifying robot. Read the exact support and bumper criteria before specifying a climb.

The Power Cube is not a 2023 foam cube. The manual describes a nylon-covered HDPE crate approximately 13 by 13 by 11 inches and 3.25 pounds. Its open fabric-covered face, rigid edges, seams and orientation change how rollers engage. Under G22 the robot may control only one cube. An acquisition mechanism should therefore maximize rapid ownership, pose tolerance and recovery, rather than accumulate a hopper. A retained cube can be reoriented by a wrist or gripper, but a robot cannot solve a long route with bulk storage.

## What can and cannot be independently owned

AUTO QUEST requires all three robots to complete AUTO-RUN and the alliance to own its switch at the end of auto. One robot can own the switch requirement and its own movement, but cannot directly cause a disabled partner's line crossing. FACE THE BOSS requires three physical climbs, or two physical climbs plus LEVITATE. A robot that can carry one partner and supply LEVITATE cubes owns much of the engineering burden, while retaining partner mounting and human-player execution dependencies. Record those residual dependencies explicitly. Do not label either entire condition guaranteed solo RP.

For 1833, the transferable objective is a primary robot that can win the scale race, protect its switch and complete the attainable bonus work with weak partners. It is not a switch-only support design. Historical specialists remain useful mechanism references and counterexamples. A primary robot can spend a particular playoff match on an opposing switch without having been designed with a low capability ceiling.

The two switches are independent. Scoring on the opponent's switch denies their ownership points; it does not make that switch score for you. Scale ownership, by contrast, is contested by both alliances. In a hypothetical 20-second teleop window, changing the scale from opponent-owned to yours can improve the relative score by roughly 40 recurring points, before acquisition-transition details and powerups. Merely stopping their switch for the same window denies roughly 20 recurring points. These are conditional marginal values, not a permanent 2:1 rule: a scale you cannot hold may be a worse investment than a short, repeatable switch attack.

Likewise, an extra cube on a securely owned scale has little immediate scoring value but can buy reserve against an opposing cycle. The useful question is how many seconds of future ownership it protects, and at what opportunity cost. A cube added to an already hopelessly lost scale can have effectively zero ownership return. The agent must calculate the catch-up deficit, available inventory, competing cycle rates, and remaining time before recommending another scale cycle.

## Spatial economy and why acquisition changed the ceiling

The finite field supply begins in fence rows, portals and protected pyramids. Early accessible cubes are different from late portal cycles. A mechanism that cleanly removes one pyramid cube without scattering the others preserves access and can protect the following autonomous acquisition. A pickup that succeeds eventually but disorganizes the inventory may lower the entire alliance's subsequent throughput. Any claimed four-cube autonomous depends on both path execution and the state left by the previous pickup.

A full cycle includes approach, capture, confirmation, reorientation, transport, lift, placement and escape. Some motions overlap: raising an elevator while driving can save time, but it changes stability and may require acceleration limits. Front/back scoring can remove a chassis turn; it also requires a collision-free pass-through and controlled retention during rotation. A mechanism is valuable when that saved turn survives the full cycle, not because the wrist can spin impressively on a stand.

An elevator's maximum reach alone is insufficient. Scale height changes with balance, and accumulated cubes make the target a pile rather than a flat empty pan. The robot may need both rapid ejection and accurate placement, especially when a rushed cube can rebound, fall, or destabilize previously scored cubes. Cube orientation affects packing and effective pile height. 148 explicitly designed its boot intake to normalize orientation. A camera-based estimate of scale attitude can reduce unnecessary lift travel, as 254's binder describes, but vision latency and occlusion remain interfaces to handle.

Tangent-to-route acceleration, turn behavior and traversal over the scale platform matter more than unconstrained top speed. A tall loaded elevator raises overturning moment; a mechanism advertised as fast may force the driver to brake early or wait to lower before accelerating. Chassis wheel placement, lift setback, battery position, deployed forks, and a partner's mass during climbing must be examined as a common load system. Do not copy a drive gearing value without the original wheel size, motor assumptions and acceleration policy.

## Powerups: a scheduling and opportunity-cost problem

LEVITATE costs three vault cubes and credits one climb up to the alliance maximum. Those cubes also earn their normal vault points. It therefore offers a different package of value from simply comparing 30 climb points with 15 vault points. FORCE grants ownership for 10 seconds: one cube targets the switch, two the scale, three both. BOOST doubles ownership points for 10 seconds on the analogous targets, but depends on actually earning ownership. Each powerup can be played only once. Additional cubes after activation can still earn vault points under the manual's rules.

The global FORCE/BOOST queue is a subtle constraint: these powerups do not simply overlap freely because different alliances press buttons. A powerup request can wait for the current one to expire. A timing plan must include both alliances' queue and the remaining match time. Never award a full 10-second benefit to a powerup that cannot finish before the match ends, or assume BOOST guarantees ownership while a plate is lost.

The vault has three columns holding up to three cubes each, so it is a finite nine-cube scoring destination rather than an unlimited five-points-per-cube outlet. Playing FORCE or BOOST early at a lower level does not permit replaying or upgrading that powerup later. Additional legal cubes can still fill the column for vault points. Capacity and activation are separate states (manual physical pages 29–30 and 41–42).

There is no universal instruction to fill the vault first. In a contested match, cubes directed to powerups are cubes not establishing a durable scale lead or interrupting the opponent's switch. The marginal comparison changes once a lead is safe, a comeback is impossible, or a powerup can secure a critical final interval. The correct decision is state-dependent, with a human player and drive coach coordinating execution.

## Legal contact and release locations shape the mechanism

Under G09, launching a cube is permitted only in specified relationships to the intended scale plate, switch or exchange: the scale condition uses the alliance's null territory, the switch condition uses fence contact/intersection, and the exchange condition uses the exchange zone. A historical roller's ability to eject quickly is therefore not a general permission for long-range scoring. Approach geometry and legal release position belong in the cycle model (physical pages 53–54).

G16 protects a robot meeting its own null-territory conditions from opposing contact. G18 protects qualifying platform-zone robots during endgame, with a climb-credit consequence. G12 also constrains coordinated shutdown of major gameplay access, while G14 and G15 govern pinning and exchange blocking. The championship account of portal defense must be read within those limits, not as permission to camp anywhere indefinitely or block all supplies with several robots. This shapes which paths can be reliably contested and which targets are protected once approached correctly (physical pages 55–56).

## Documented evolution, with limits on the historical claim

The most concrete before/after evidence in this expansion is mechanism-specific rather than a complete week-by-week census. Team 1678's [2018 CAD release, replies 8 and 12](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/team-1678-citrus-circuits-2018-cad-release/166149) distinguishes its earlier horizontal roller intake from a later side-to-side design adapted from actual 1323 CAD. The later intake was intentionally omitted from the public assembly. This is evidence of design transfer and a revision; it is not permission to invent the missing CAD or claim a measured cycle improvement.

2898's binder separately documents an initial scale-capable elevator robot, failures involving reach/alignment/sensors, and a switch/exchange rebuild that retained the intake and drivebase. That is an instructive recovery under the contemporary bag-and-tag constraints. Its narrowed role is not 1833's desired kickoff objective. The transferable lesson is to detect architecture-interface risks before expensive manufacture, and to preserve useful modules if recovery becomes necessary. “This team rebuilt” does not imply rebuilding is cheap.

At the elite endpoint, [254's championship account](https://blog.team254.com/2018cmp/) describes choosing between scale auto and combined switch/scale auto based on partner confidence. Its Houston playoff plan combined scale ownership, attack on the opponent's switch, and interruption of portal supply. It also reports deliberately limited exchange investment. This is a team account of its own strategy, not a visual audit of every Einstein action. The causal interpretation is that control of inventory access and competing scoring clocks can dominate simply maximizing the number of cubes placed in one target.

254's binder provides an unusually direct chain from first-seed ambition to autonomous output, all-target capability and a partner lift. That chain resembles 1833's wish to control qualification outcomes, while the exact 2018 implementation uses historical pneumatic hardware that must not be copied into a current 1833 recommendation. Do not infer that a no-turret preference means all lift-and-wrist complexity is justified; the saved turns must repay the complete integration burden.

Houston and Detroit were separate championship fields. The [Houston Einstein record](https://www.thebluealliance.com/event/2018cmptx) identifies the 254/148/2976/3075 championship alliance. The [Detroit record](https://www.thebluealliance.com/event/2018cmpmi) is a different tournament and includes Stryke Force's alliance. Treat the winners and match scores as event facts; do not use the Houston team's tactical report as an explanation of Detroit matches. This edition does not add individual visual audits, new PCH benchmarks, or an EPA-selected 25-team cohort for 2018.

## Mechanism reference map and transfer conditions

| Demand | References in this expansion | What the agent should actually borrow |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capture a rigid, covered box in varied poses | 2018-148, 2018-254, 2018-1678, 2018-1610, 2018-2898 | Contact geometry, orientation control, compliant capture and a retained state; verify surface/material differences |
| Reach high without carrying unnecessary mass | 2018-148, 2018-254, 2018-1610 | Rigging, bearing arrangement, lift overlap and pass-through; derive load and stiffness again |
| Reduce turns through front/back scoring | 2018-254, 2018-1678 | Collision-free wrist/lift path and retained-piece control, including loaded CG |
| Explore an arm instead of an elevator | 2018-971, 2018-2898 V2 | Workspace and drive-mounted mass; the latter does not establish high-target reach |
| Traverse while moving sideways | 2018-2910 | Clearance and contact geometry, not the assumption that swerve clears every obstacle |
| Lift a partner | 2018-148, 2018-254, 2018-1678 | Partner capture and reaction load path; residual docking dependency and actuator adaptation |

The new game must be decomposed before any of these references earns priority. A box-shaped piece does not make the game POWER UP, and tall scoring does not automatically require a multi-stage elevator. Start with scoring states, possession rules, travel distances, target workspace, accuracy, denial and bonus prerequisites. Only then compare coherent mechanisms.

## Useful first-pass calculations

Write `Tcycle = Tacquire + Ttravel + Tplace + Tescape − Toverlap`, with every term defined and a separate recovery allowance. For ownership, estimate the area under the alliance ownership indicator over time rather than points per cube. Keep the probability of a failed pickup, the time cost of recovery and the chance a cube remains scored separate. For lifts, calculate force and power through the actual rigging, spool radius, moving-stage masses and efficiency; a motor count and gear ratio copied from a binder are not a new design calculation.

For a steady forward acceleration, compare overturning moment `m a h` with gravitational restoring moment `m g b`, where `h` is loaded system CG height and `b` is distance from the CG projection to the relevant support edge. This is a screening calculation, not a contact-impact or dynamic proof. In the real robot the cube, moving carriage and any partner alter both terms. A targeted test should address the unresolved boundary that could reverse an architecture choice, after the cheaper envelope and load checks have been done.

Read the full robot packets and the [cross-season transfer guide](HISTORICAL_2018_2019_TRANSFER.md) before turning this context into a recommendation.

name: DESTINATION: DEEP SPACE

# 2019 — DESTINATION: DEEP SPACE

## A finite set of coupled scoring states

DEEP SPACE combines hatch installation, cargo delivery, blind initial operation and a climb onto stepped platforms. Its repeated cycle is not equivalent to pouring more objects into a common goal. Every useful destination has a state: an empty hatch location, a retained panel with an empty bay, a completed panel/cargo pair, or a location already occupied. A robot that handles only one piece type can exhaust its useful targets or become dependent on another robot's prerequisites.

The governing rules source here is the [official 133-page manual](https://firstfrc.blob.core.windows.net/frc2019/Manual/2019FRCGameSeasonManual.pdf), notably physical PDF pages 22–34, 39–43 and 52–60. This is an archived assembled manual; verify the governing update/Q&A for a particular competition. All illustrative throughput and marginal calculations below are analysis, not claimed observations of specific matches.

The first 15 seconds are SANDSTORM: driver view is blocked, but a team may use autonomous behavior, cameras or blind driving. Do not describe it as an autonomous-only phase or apply a different piece scoring multiplier. Leaving from HAB level 1 earns 3 and from level 2 earns 6 when the crossing conditions are met. The remaining 135 seconds are normal driver control. A hatch panel is worth 2 and a retained cargo is worth 3. End-of-match HAB levels 1/2/3 are worth 3/6/12. Complete Rocket requires six scored panels and six cargo in one rocket; HAB Docking requires at least 15 climb points. Each grants one qualification RP, in addition to match result RP. These bonuses do not carry into playoffs.

Hatch retention is a real prerequisite. A cargo counts only in a bay with a scored hatch or null hatch, under the manual's final-state criteria. Cargo ship bay floors initially retain cargo but move at the end of sandstorm; this creates a trap for naive initial-phase scoring arithmetic. Null hatches permit retained cargo without their own 2-point panel credit, and their placement/preload rules must be considered separately. Do not add an actual panel's 2 points again when cargo goes into that bay.

The cargo is a roughly 13-inch inflatable rubber ball, with inflation, seams, wear and compliance affecting capture. A hatch is a thin, broad disk with a center opening and hook/loop scoring interface. Its planar alignment and release requirements are unlike ball ejection. G4 limits control to one game piece total, including control through other objects. A piece at least partly supported by a rocket or cargo ship is excluded from robot control; this is not permission to carry a hatch and a cargo together. Read the examples on physical pages 53–54 before planning acquisition transitions. This edition does not recommend a bulk-storage architecture for this game.

## Separate ranking architecture from playoff route selection

A complete rocket contains 30 piece points: `6×2 + 6×3`. The RP can be strategically valuable beyond those 30 points because qualification ranking determines alliance selection leverage. A robot aiming to own that condition needs both piece types and all three levels, plus access to both faces. It must deliver a complete sequence in the available time while defending against drops, travel variance and disruption. “Can reach level 3” is a geometric capability, not a solo-rocket demonstration.

The HAB RP has an especially important dependency boundary. A single level-3 climb earns 12, below the threshold of 15. One partner reaching level 1 supplies the remaining 3, or a partner-carry mechanism can own more of the mechanical task. A robot that climbs level 3 alone cannot truthfully claim to solo HAB Docking with no other robot involved. A partner lift replaces a demanding partner climb with docking, weight, geometry and coordination requirements; it does not make the partner cease to exist.

For 1833, independent completion of the rocket is an architectural objective worth evaluating, while unavoidable partner conditions should be quantified instead of wished away. A lower-level cargo-only robot can be effective in an alliance, but it is not an acceptable default support-only design for this team. Conversely, a primary robot may choose fast low cargo cycles during a playoff match once its partners and target allocation are known. Capability and match assignment are different decisions.

Playoffs remove bonus RP. If a low cargo-ship cycle is faster and produces the same 3 cargo points as a high rocket cycle, high reach earns value only through target availability, traffic, partner allocation or other match-specific conditions. It is incorrect to preserve a qualification rocket-filling schedule mechanically once the objective becomes winning a known playoff matchup. The design should retain broad primary capability while the coach exploits the highest marginal route at that moment.

## Work backwards from the complete task graph

Represent every rocket bay as `unpanelled → panel retained → cargo retained`. A panel-placement failure can force a retry before any cargo cycle has value. A dropped panel or cargo may change the source choice, require floor recovery, occupy legal possession, or make a planned route unavailable. One successful practice cycle says little about the probability of completing twelve ordered placements under defense.

A simple illustrative completion model is `Pcomplete = ∏ pi` only when the individual task probabilities are independent and there is no retry time. Real matches violate both assumptions. A more useful time budget includes scheduled retries and interruption: `Tremaining ≥ Σ expected task times + travel between distinct source/goal states + recovery reserve + climb`. State whether a recovery allowance is in every cycle or charged only on failures. Never quietly multiply an ideal fastest cycle by twelve.

The rocket has two faces and three levels. The lowest hatch center is 19 inches, with 28-inch vertical separation to the next levels, per the field description. These are panel-center references, not universal cargo release heights. A useful workspace includes approach standoff, bumper offsets, panel compliance, the path to loading-station height and collision clearance through every transition. An elevator that passes a ball through its uprights must clear the true compressed and off-center ball, the end effector and cable path, not just a nominal sphere in a single CAD pose.

At a loading station, firm panel retention and clean release often matter more than an elaborate wrist. The gripper must tolerate the panel's source pose, hold during acceleration/impacts, align the scoring plane, transfer to hook/loop, and detach without pulling the panel off again. Expanding fingers through the center opening, compliant wheel gripping, and suction solve different interfaces. They should be compared using approach tolerance, retained load, release delay, recoverability, power, sensing and service burden.

## Legal defense and height limits change reachable routes

G9 allows no more than one robot at or beyond the opponent's cargo-ship line, subject to its forced-crossing exception. G10 limits extension beyond the frame while a robot is completely beyond that line, and G11 limits throwing cargo there. These are spatially defined conditions, not a blanket statement that only one robot anywhere may make defensive contact. G3 prevents crossing the opponent's cargo-ship line during sandstorm. A route model should include where a defender can legally engage and how its own mechanisms must be stowed (physical pages 53–55).

G5 prohibits removing opponents' scored pieces, with a rocket-RP consequence in specified circumstances; the game is not a general descore contest. G13 protects opponents fully inside their HAB zone, with additional climb-credit consequences late in the match. G12 limits robot height in either HAB zone to the alliance-wall height, and G24 limits extension beyond the frame. An architecture needs legal folded and extended states through the route, not only a reachable scoring pose (physical pages 54–59). These boundaries are important when deciding whether high reach, a long arm or a particular climb can coexist with quick travel.

## Handoff versus carrying the ground intake

A chassis-mounted floor collector plus a smaller elevator gripper can reduce moving mass. The collector crosses the bumper, captures cargo and hands it into the scoring mechanism. The extra transfer creates a new failure state, so the net cycle improvement is not automatic. If the lift gripper and collector overlap in motion, the robot needs sensing and interlocks to distinguish “captured,” “ready for handoff,” “transferring” and “secure to raise.” A ball pinched between the mechanisms can cause a false success or jam.

1610 explicitly chose this trade: more total mechanism weight in exchange for less traveling up the elevator. Its binder also describes substantial lift weight reduction from thinner and smaller tubing. Neither observation proves an arbitrary thin tube is stiff enough, or that a ground collector should always be separate. Arm bending, bearing spacing, off-center loads, deceleration and retained-piece shock still determine the acceptable structure.

971's 2019 slides show a floor roller and a compact suction wrist, a lightweight carbon-fiber lift, and a small drivebase. The slides are visual and textual evidence; they are not a narrated transcript. Vacuum grip depends on leak flow, cup conformity, contact load and release behavior. It is not enough to multiply atmospheric pressure by a nominal cup area and call that the defended retention force. A cup on a curved ball can peel under moment even when a flat-plate axial calculation looks generous.

Team 125's [detailed rejected-prototype account](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/suction-and-vacuum/368009/13) is valuable negative evidence. Its team author describes promising hatch handling but concerns about cargo retention under collisions and floor-loader handoff. The team moved to wheels. This does not prove suction was bad on every robot; it shows why the whole acquisition-to-score sequence and defended loading cases must determine a choice.

## The no-turret transfer boundary

254's Backlash used a yawing superstructure in addition to lift, shoulder and wrist. The binder ties that choice to reducing chassis turns and scoring while managing defense. Preserve that historical reason accurately. It does not override 1833's prohibition on turrets. The useful extraction may be a compact dual-piece end effector, drive-mounted motors, joint counterbalance or collision sequencing. A current design must solve heading and approach using chassis motion or another permitted arrangement, and account for the resulting cycle time.

Removing one axis from a historical robot is not a harmless edit. It changes reachable poses, target-facing time, intake presentation and legal perimeter transitions. Compare a fixed-plane pass-through elevator/wrist with a fixed-plane articulated arm using the same source/goal sequence and defended routes. A visually simpler assembly may still require more driver alignment or slower transitions. A visually complex historical robot may contain one excellent simple subsystem worth borrowing without copying the whole machine.

## Documented seasonal development

254's [2019 binder](https://media.team254.com/resources/Team_254_Tech_Binder_2019.pdf), physical pages 9–12 and 20–30, supplies explicit evolution rather than a timeless final snapshot. It describes a shorter pre-Champs arm and larger regional intake, then a longer, lighter arm and smaller championship intake. The team links the changes to torque/current problems, reach and swept volume. Its earlier stinger climb loaded the arm/wrist, while the later suction climb used a different reaction path and elevator power; some brakes consequently became unnecessary. Do not combine the former climber's load assumptions with the final intake and claim that hybrid competed.

The same source describes sandstorm moving from substantial driver involvement toward a tuned autonomous routine by championship. The strategic implication is a reduction in acquisition/alignment variance and driver camera burden, not a bonus multiplier. An agent should compare actual time and reliability, and distinguish a desired routine from one used in competition.

2910's [CAD discussion](https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/2910-cad-release-2019/357461) records motor protection after early contact damage and later HAB support changes developed for sharing platform space. It is evidence of design revision and packaging tradeoffs. Its [championship report](https://frcteam2910.org/2019/04/25/2019-world-championships/) also documents a qualification seed below its ambition and an early playoff exit. A high-quality robot is not immune to schedule, failures or ranking variance. Do not misidentify 2910 as the 2019 Houston championship winner because of a practice climb with 1323.

Citrus's 2019 CAD release explicitly says a modeled elevator brake was scrapped and never installed on the competition robot. Its published robot page describes scoring both piece types on all levels and lifting two partners. These illustrate two different kinds of evidence: a competition-capability report and a precise disconfirmation of a CAD feature. Neither grants an exhaustive chronology of every climb mechanism revision or an independently verified “only team” claim.

Houston and Detroit must remain separate. [Houston Einstein](https://www.thebluealliance.com/event/2019cmptx) includes 1323/973/5026 and 254's different alliance. [Detroit Einstein](https://www.thebluealliance.com/event/2019cmpmi) is a separate event with 3707/217/4481 in its winning final series. Scores and rosters establish outcomes, not how each robot scored or defended. This expansion supplies no new match-by-match visual audit or validated causal account of all Einstein tactics.

## Endgame is space as well as points

HAB level 3's physical footprint makes coexistence important. A robot that occupies less top surface can preserve another robot's scoring opportunity, sometimes more effectively than physically lifting it. 254 explored suction at an edge; 2910 documented supports that kept bumpers legally above the level while hanging more of the robot off. The design variable is the complete support polygon and load path, not the label “climb.”

The incremental value of level 3 instead of level 2 is 6 points. That equals two retained cargo in simple scoring arithmetic, but whether those cargo can actually be delivered in the saved time depends on remaining bays, panel state, routes, defense and the reliability of the alternate climb. Similarly, leaving 10 seconds early for a climb may forfeit a complete panel/cargo cycle or almost nothing if targets are saturated. Do not import the 2026 conclusion that climbing was low priority into this game's bonus structure.

For 1833, historical pneumatic kicks, brakes and deploying cylinders remain disallowed as recommended actuation. Adapt the geometry with an electric or justified passive mechanism, then redo holding, release, load transfer, hard stops, failure recovery and legal support checks. An electrically driven vacuum pump is a separate historical pressure system and is not automatic permission to introduce a pneumatic baseline.

## How to use this chapter for a genuinely new game

Begin with a state graph of legal piece transformations and target occupancy, identify the requirements the robot can truly own, and write a timed weak-partner scenario. Then compare acquisition, retained pose, reach, transition count, electrical burden and serviceability. Use the [transfer guide](HISTORICAL_2018_2019_TRANSFER.md) and complete robot packets to retrieve mechanisms by function. A game with boxes and multiple heights may share acquisition mechanics with 2018 and workspaces with 2019 or 2023, while having entirely different scoring incentives. The historical label must never substitute for reading the new manual.

name: RAPID REACT
analysis_markdown:
# 2022 — RAPID REACT

RAPID REACT is a two-cargo-possession, repeated-acquisition game around a shared central hub, followed by a multi-step climbing task. The strategic unit is a successful collect–aim–release cycle under traffic. Cargo keeps returning to play, so the output ceiling is primarily time, access, accuracy and possession management rather than a fixed set of high-value nodes.

The [official manual](https://firstfrc.blob.core.windows.net/frc2022/Manual/HTML/2022FRCGameManual.htm) assigns upper-hub cargo 4 points in autonomous and 2 in teleop; lower cargo is 2/1. Taxi is 2. Hangar levels are 4/6/10/15. Qualifications add cargo and hangar bonuses: normally 20 scored cargo, reduced to 18 by the autonomous quintet, and 16 hangar points. These are alliance conditions. A robot need not independently supply the whole threshold.

## Core demands and marginal value

An upper-hub scorer needs to collect quickly enough that aim and feed matter. A high-output launcher supplied slowly is just an expensive waiting mechanism. With only two owned cargo in possession, a wide collector is chiefly a reduction in acquisition time and driver precision; a deep hopper has little strategic value. A good database query therefore asks for pickup recovery, two-ball singulation and release delay before asking which flywheel is fastest.

Fixed-heading, hooded and turreted architectures solve different route problems. A turret can preserve aim while the chassis collects or avoids a defender. A fixed launcher can exchange that flexibility for mass, simplicity or a powerful climb. Neither wins categorically: shot locations, defended accuracy, range-map quality and time spent rotating determine the effective difference. The 2046, 694 and 118 dossiers deliberately preserve those contrasts.

A traversal climb is worth 15 points, equivalent to 7.5 ordinary teleop upper cargo. The incremental comparison is often smaller: moving from a reliable high climb to traversal adds only 5 points. A new traversal mechanism is justified by that increment, its successful-completion probability, the cycling time surrendered and its interaction with partners. A ten-second faster climb can be valuable even without a higher rung because it returns usable scoring time earlier in the match. Conversely, a spectacular fast offseason sequence cannot establish the onseason tradeoff.

## How the strategic problem developed

The reviewed robot histories show several simultaneous development paths rather than a single universal meta. Teams improved collector materials and centering, expanded autonomous routines, automated distance shooting, added moving-shot compensation and changed climbs. For example, 5940's late technical interview includes an offseason traversal mechanism; its onseason high-bar choice must remain a separate state. 4911's hardware and vision capability also arrived on different timelines. This matters when asking what was feasible at week 3.

As collection and autonomous improved, midfield supply and defended shot quality became increasingly important. A robot can contribute by disrupting the opponent's two-cargo flow, forcing an extra turn, or occupying a comfortable shooting location. Defending is worthwhile only if denied points exceed the defender's forgone scoring, its extra penalty risk and any interference imposed on its own scorers. A mechanism database cannot settle that calculation without a match role and opponent.

The [254 Championship retrospective](https://blog.team254.com/2022cmp/) supplies a concrete late-season example. Its finals account describes changing the third robot to 3175 for opponent-cargo retention and adjusting offensive positioning against 4099. This is a role and supply adaptation, not a wholesale replacement of the scoring mechanisms. It illustrates why an alliance can improve without adding another primary scorer.

The separate Einstein records expose other tradeoffs. Match 3 has equal recorded autonomous and cargo-teleop totals, with the clean-score gap entirely in endgame. Match 8 has a much larger teleop advantage that survives an endgame deficit. These are descriptive decompositions, not proofs that a particular strategic decision caused the result. The archived captions sometimes describe traffic or defensive pursuit; visual attribution remains an explicit follow-up task.

## Architecture recommendations this season can teach

For a resource-limited upper-hub robot, first establish a broad reliable pickup, a two-ball path that never releases accidentally, a repeatable shot region and a climb that completes with generous deadline margin. Add range flexibility when the real defended route requires it. A color-rejection system must handle both sensing delay and possession sequencing; detecting an opponent ball is not the same as rejecting it without losing an owned one.

For a top-alliance role, prioritize compatible autonomous paths, sustained accuracy after contact and a climb layout that permits partners to finish too. Use the 2481 truss-driving system as an alternative kinematic family, not a plug-in attachment: its frame and approach geometry commit the whole robot to that choice. Use 118 for turret/feed integration, 254 for complete cargo flow and climb packaging, and 5940/5172 for histories in which the later mechanism is not the original competition configuration.

PCH week-3, week-5 and DCMP comparisons should use the matching event snapshot. The championship-winning architecture is a useful ceiling reference; its final season EPA is not an estimate of what a March robot already achieved. See `benchmarks.csv` for the actual stage-specific comparisons.


# RAPID REACT: why a two-ball robot is a logistics system

This is an additional analytical layer to the 2022 game chapter, not a replacement for its rules and event data. Treat the named robots as documented examples, the RoboReplay material as attributed retrospective interpretation and the causal arguments below as engineering hypotheses to test. There is no claim that reviewing transcripts substitutes for a frame-by-frame match audit.

## Small possession capacity makes the entire field part of the mechanism

A limited onboard inventory means that intake direction, acquisition tolerance, heading changes, rejected opponent cargo and shot location continually reshape the next cycle. A robot can have a fast flywheel and still spend most of its useful time with no shootable cargo. The source question is therefore not just how fast a ball leaves a wheel. It is how quickly the robot can obtain the next useful pair without rotating, crossing an occupied lane or getting trapped in a predictable collection pattern.

The 254 dossier provides a package with opposed collectors, serialization, opponent-color handling, a turret and a traversal system. Read those functions together. Either-side collection can reduce chassis turning; the serializer must reconcile two directions of arrival; rejection must remove unwanted cargo without losing useful possession or creating an unexpected path; the turret must permit a sensible shooting direction after the chassis chooses an acquisition route. The benefit is joint, and each interface can consume the time that the other mechanisms appear to save. [254’s technical binder](https://media.team254.com/2022/10/8f2407a5-Team_254_Tech_Binder_2022.pdf).

An architecture agent should represent the field as a changing inventory of accessible cargo, not a permanent set of equally available balls. Cargo next to an opposing robot is different from cargo at an unobstructed wall; cargo of the wrong color can occupy valuable acquisition time; a ball just returned by the hub can be useful only if someone can see and reach it. Even a good color-rejection system needs a policy for when to reject and where to send the ball. The tactical value of removing an opponent’s piece depends on how much extra time the opponent must spend recovering it and whether the action displaces a useful scoring opportunity of your own.

## Turret value depends on what the chassis can keep doing

Independent azimuth can make otherwise inconvenient acquisition headings useful. It can also preserve a shot while the chassis translates. But the system needs usable angular range, cable management, a reliable state estimate and repeatable exit conditions. A fast collector paired with a turret that must unwind at the wrong time can have lower effective output than a simpler machine with an easier route. A field-relative shooting solution paired with inconsistent feeder contact can miss for reasons that appear to be localization errors.

The design test should therefore record acquisition-to-shot time under several approach headings and disturbances. Include a forced reversal, a ball entering from the less convenient side, an opponent-color rejection and a shot immediately after a collision. These are not arbitrary stress tests: they examine whether the decoupling benefit survives the situations that make decoupling valuable in the first place. A shooter with an excellent stationary calibration does not establish that result.

Compare robots at a similar operating condition. A two-ball burst at a favorable range, a moving shot after contact and a full match with resource denial are different observations. The database’s match phase data cannot identify which mechanism caused a score difference. For that, retrieve the footage and distinguish an aim error from an empty robot, a disabled mechanism, a driver choosing defense or a partner occupying a route.

## Climbing changes the final scoring policy

The hangar makes endgame an exercise in mechanism loads, alliance packing and timing. A fast high-value climb can release additional time for cargo, while an elaborate climb that requires an early departure may sacrifice the points it was meant to add. The comparison is against the cargo that would actually remain available, not the robot’s best unconstrained cycle. The marginal value of another cycle changes when a partner has already removed nearby cargo, a defender controls the return path or the robot has lost an intake.

A traversal shortcut that reacts against field structure can avoid visiting every intermediate position, but it also changes the load path and failure consequences. Borrowing the visible hook or stinger without studying how the chassis, carriage and reaction member carry the load is incomplete. Simultaneous climbs also need clearance and ordering; a solo demonstration does not establish that the third partner can enter late or that loaded structures will avoid one another.

For strategic design, specify a distribution of approach-to-confirmed-climb times and the recovery procedure after the first missed engagement. A team should know whether its climb is still worthwhile after a delayed approach, not merely whether it can complete an ideal practice sequence. An agent should include the points and time surrendered if it fails, and the expected impact on partners waiting to use the same structure.

## What the finals analysis adds, and what it cannot prove

RoboReplay’s retrospective of Einstein final 1 discusses defense on 1577, changed cleanup demands, pressure on 254 and late shooting/climbing decisions. These connect mechanism capability with the opponent’s choices, but the narrator’s estimates of denied shots and intent remain commentary. The season-recap video also revisits 2022 and advances a disputed three-second possession interpretation. That passage is retained as a disagreement requiring official rules, not as an allowable design trick. See the reviews for `c5rvL_wVdXc` and `1UsbJD-zRjU` in the ledger.

The broad analytical question is whether the alliance can maintain useful scoring when the opponent attacks its supply rather than its flywheel. If one robot absorbs defense and another becomes the main cleaner, their observed scoring changes without either mechanism becoming intrinsically better or worse. That is why copying the highest match output without recording role is dangerous. The same robot may be a scorer, a resource-denial platform or a late-climb insurance policy in different matches.

## A PCH interpretation

Use the historical PCH samples to locate the field’s demonstrated output, then build a role-specific target. For a likely captain, ask whether your robot can continue producing under the defense it will attract and whether it has autonomous routines that leave useful cargo and routes for partners. For a complementary pick, ask whether it can acquire the cargo the captain avoids, supply a reliable endgame contribution or defend while preserving a low penalty rate. These roles can demand different intake width, size and control investment even within the same game.

The 2022 references do not justify importing a large 2026 hopper: the possession structure and scoring windows are different. What transfers is the method of maintaining controlled flow and reducing unnecessary motion. The agent should extract those principles while discarding season-specific assumptions about legal storage, target geometry and opponent-color handling. The best historical analogy is the one that identifies both the useful similarity and the rule or field feature that breaks the analogy.
